name: Lip lift (bullhorn / subnasal)
lead: A lip lift is a surgical procedure that shortens the vertical distance between the base of the nose and the upper lip by removing a strip of skin, which raises the lip and shows more of the vermilion, the pink part of the lip. In the subnasal or "bullhorn" version the incision follows the underside of the nose, so the scar sits in the crease where the nose meets the lip [1][3][8].

People seek it for a long upper lip, a short or thin-looking upper vermilion, or too little tooth show at rest. Surgeons describe the aesthetic aim as a shorter nose-to-lip distance, more visible vermilion and a few millimetres of upper tooth display, features often grouped under a youthful or feminine lip [8][9]. In looksmaxxing communities the operation is discussed as a "hardmaxx" fix for a long philtrum, with posters linking the philtrum to ideas such as chin-to-philtrum ratio and midface proportions [18].

The procedure has been described in plastic surgery journals since the early 1980s [5][4][3]. The published literature consists mainly of surgeon case series and technique reviews, including a 2023 systematic review of upper lip lifting techniques that included nine studies [10]. The main trade-off discussed in that literature is a permanent scar, which surgeons try to conceal in the subnasal crease [3][10].

angle.text: A lip lift physically shortens the skin between nose and upper lip. People use it to get a shorter philtrum, a fuller-looking upper lip without filler and more tooth show at rest.

paras: The upper lip has a cutaneous (skin) portion between the base of the nose and the vermilion border. Aging and individual anatomy can lengthen this segment, which reduces the visible pink of the lip and the amount of tooth shown at rest [4][11]. A lip lift excises a shaped strip of skin, often an ellipse with a wavy or gull-wing outline, and closes the gap so the lip sits higher [3][1].

A review of the subnasal lift describes it as removal of an ellipse of skin and subcutaneous tissue immediately below the nostril base, performed alone or alongside other rejuvenation procedures [11]. Because the incision follows the nasal sill, the scar lies in a natural shadow under the nose [3].

Reviews classify lip lifts into direct and indirect types, plus corner-of-mouth lifts and V-Y advancement. The direct (gull-wing) lift removes tissue at or just above the white roll along the vermilion border; the indirect lift removes tissue under the nose, with the bullhorn as its best-known form [1].

Other described variants include the corner ("smile") lift, which resects tissue above the mouth corners, a thread lift that is described as short-lived, and a V-Y advancement that works from inside the mouth [1]. A 2019 article describes a modified deep-plane bullhorn technique that attaches the lift to deeper tissue layers, and the author's series of 823 patients is reported in its title [12]. A 2022 review emphasises designing the incision to respect anatomy and placing the tension deep to the dermis so the skin incision carries less pull [9].

Surgical reviews say patient selection depends on lip height, vermilion height, alar base width, skin type, upper incisor show and maxillary height, and that precise measurement and careful skin closure help minimise a visible scar [8]. The 2023 systematic review found that studies measure lifting in different ways, either as photographic ratios or as caliper-measured heights, which makes results hard to compare directly [10].

Wikipedia notes that surgeons developed lip-lifting and augmentation techniques in the 1980s, when collagen, then the main lip filler, was limited in producing lasting change [1]. A 1981 British Journal of Plastic Surgery paper titled "Lip lifting" is among the earliest indexed reports [5]. A 1984 Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery paper described lifting and everting thin lips along the vermilion border and reported 32 cases [4]. A 1986 paper described removing a wavy ellipse of skin, hiding the scar under the nose and reported 83 patients [3].

A 1992 Clinics in Plastic Surgery review covered rejuvenation of the aging mouth [7], and a 2009 Aesthetic Surgery Journal paper reported 28 years of experience with direct excision [6]. By the 2000s and 2010s, review articles described the subnasal lift as simple but practised by a limited number of surgeons [11], and later reviews addressed it in the context of facial feminization and orthognathic planning [13][14][15]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference whose claims are unverified, attributes a first description to 1971 and credits social media with a rise in interest since the 2010s [2].

Published evidence is mainly surgeon-authored case series and technique reviews. The 1986 report described minimal scars and excellent results in 83 patients [3]. The 1984 report on thin lips described a vermilion-border technique in 32 patients [4]. The 2009 report summarised 28 years of direct excision for the aging mouth [6].

A 2023 systematic review in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery searched MEDLINE, EMBASE and Cochrane and included nine studies from 495 hits, eight surgical and one nonsurgical. It reported that surgical techniques appeared to last longer than nonsurgical ones, that patient satisfaction was good with no severe complaints, and that quantitative methods differed between studies. The authors rated the level of evidence as III [10]. A separate Europe PMC record describes Talei's 2019 modified bullhorn technique and its 823-patient series [12].

Facial feminization surgery reviews list lip shortening among the procedures offered to some transgender women and to some non-transgender women who want a more feminine face [15][13]. A registered trial (NCT06104514, 60 participants, completed) tested the Sofwave energy device for lifting the upper lip and softening perioral lines, a nonsurgical comparison [17]. No randomized trial of the surgical lip lift has been identified.

Reviews describe the lip lift as an add-on to facial rejuvenation [11], to feminization procedures such as rhinoplasty and brow work [13][15], and to orthognathic surgery planning, where adjunctive aesthetic procedures aim to improve facial balance [14]. Forum members likewise report bundling a lip lift with other surgeries on trips abroad, for example with chin surgery, cheek implants and brow lifts [21][22].

Wikipedia lists numbness, stiffness, pain, paraesthesia, lip distortion, lip lengthening, smile deformation, speech changes and visible scarring as possible complications, and describes asymmetry, under-correction and hypertrophic scarring [1]. It also reports that removing skin at or just above the white roll has been linked to scarring and stiffness, and that swelling typically eases over one to two weeks while tightness can last two to four months after a gull-wing lift [1].

The 2023 systematic review summarised a trade-off between longer-lasting surgical results and the scar they leave [10]. One poster on looksmax.org described heavy facial swelling for four to five days and little visible change by day eight [18]. Another thread asks whether gum contouring can address too much gum show after a lift, and a separate one asks whether the operation can precede jaw surgery [20][23].

Lip filler adds volume to the lips but does not change the length of the philtrum [1][2]. Lip reduction is a separate in-office procedure that removes mucosa along the wet-dry border for people who want less lip volume [16]. Nonsurgical energy-device lifting is under investigation as a temporary option [17]. A looksmax.org thread points to a clinic offering a nonsurgical philtrum-shortening service and asks whether it suits people with a long philtrum [19].

On looksmax.org, results threads are often titled by weeks after surgery and include before-and-after photos. In one, the poster reported shortening the philtrum from about 2 cm to 1.5 cm, said it changed perceived eye spacing, midface ratio and lip thickness, described using concealer-type makeup on the scar and reported paying roughly 450-500 USD abroad [18]. The thread's title calls it the only lip lift result on the forum, which suggests that posted results were relatively rare at that time [18].

Other threads ask whether the surgery is suitable at age 15 [19], seek funds for combined nose and lip surgery [24], discuss scarless or minimal-scar variants [25][26], discuss hypothetical results from photos [27], and ask how corner lifts fit into a surgical plan alongside jaw and chin implants [28]. In one reply, a poster says that roughly half of those who think they need a lip lift may need fat grafting or filler instead [19].

lore.intro: Lip lifts are discussed on looksmax.org as a way to fix a long philtrum, often alongside other facial surgeries and with before-and-after threads.[18]

claims.claim: Shortening the philtrum by a few millimetres improves several ratios at once.
claims.believers: A poster listed better midface ratio, facial width-to-height ratio, chin-to-philtrum ratio and a fuller-looking lip after removing 5 mm.[18]
claims.experts: Surgical reviews describe shortening the upper lip and increasing vermilion show; a 2023 systematic review notes studies use different measurement methods such as photographic ratios or caliper heights.[10][8]

claims.believers: The same poster said makeup concealed the scar almost entirely.[18]
claims.experts: Papers describe placing the incision beneath the nose to hide the scar, with minimal scars reported in a case series, while the systematic review lists scarring as the trade-off.[3][10]

claims.claim: Many people who want a lip lift actually need filler or fat grafting.
claims.believers: A forum reply said roughly half of those asking might do better with fat grafts or filler.[19]
claims.experts: Wikipedia and Grokipedia state that fillers add volume but do not shorten the philtrum.[1][2]

claims.claim: A lip lift can be done without a scar.
claims.believers: Threads discuss scarless or minimal-scar techniques and nonsurgical philtrum shortening.[25][20]
claims.experts: The systematic review included one nonsurgical technique and described nonsurgical options as less durable, while surgery leaves a scar.[10]

claims.claim: A lip lift is suitable for teenagers who feel their philtrum is long.
claims.believers: A 15-year-old poster said the procedure was cheap and might be possible with parental approval.[19]
claims.experts: Published lip lift literature centres on adult patients, particularly aging and feminization contexts, and does not examine teenagers.[8][4]

claims.claim: A lip lift can leave too much gum or tooth show.
claims.believers: A thread asks whether gum contouring can offset gum show after a lip lift.[29]
claims.experts: Reviews list tooth show as a planning variable and describe a few millimetres of upper tooth display as the aim.[8][9]

card.summary: Surgery that shortens a long philtrum by removing skin under the nose; permanent, with the scar as the main trade-off.
card.aka: Bullhorn lip lift, subnasal lip lift, philtrum shortening
card.note: Permanent surgery; evidence is surgeon case series.

quick.overview:
A lip lift removes a strip of skin between the nose and upper lip so the lip sits higher and more pink shows. The bullhorn version hides the scar under the nose.

Published support is surgeon case series from the 1980s onward. Forum users discuss it for long philtrums.
quick.mechanism: Skin excision shortens the philtrum and raises the vermilion. Variants differ in where the incision is placed.
quick.risks: Surgery is permanent. Scarring is the main concern in the literature; forum accounts mention swelling and uncertain results.
